newsitem.title: USA: Quality of day care affects child development.
newsitem.headline: Quality of day care affects child development.

text.p: Touching on an issue of concern to millions of working parents, U.S. researchers said on Thursday that the quality of day care was a major factor in a young child's language skills and cognitive development.
The study attempted to shift the focus of the long-running debate away from whether day care itself is good or bad and look instead at the quality of that care.
It found that if children are spoken to and responded to in a quality child-care setting, they develop the language and cognitive skills they need to be prepared for school.

An earlier phase of the study, released last year, showed that child care through the age of 15 months did not make the babies feel less secure or less attached to the mothers, as long as the mothers were giving them relatively sensitive care.

"The most striking aspects of these results from the early child-care study is that children are not being placed at a disadvantage in terms of cognitive development if they have high-quality day care in their first three years," said Dr. Duane Alexander, director of the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD).
The findings from the Study of Early Child Care were presented on Thursday in Washington at the Society for Research in Child Development.

Child care has become a pressing issue as more women stay in the work force. In 1980, 38 percent of U.S. mothers age 18-44 with a child under a year of age worked outside the home. By 1990, that had risen to 50 percent, where it remains.

One of the key indicators of quality care is the language stimulation. "We found that the amount of language that is directed at the child in child care is an important component of quality provider-child interaction," said NICHD researcher Sarah Friedman.

In quality settings, caretakers spoke to the children, answered their questions and responded to them as they spoke. In such cases, the children did well in acquiring language and cognitive skills that are "the bedrock of school readiness," Friedman said.
The skills were measured by a variety of standard tests given through age three.

In this portion of the study, the researchers also found an association, although a weak one, between the amount of time in child care and some of the mothers' behaviour. Mothers with children in child care were slightly less engaged and sensitive than those whose babies and toddlers were not in child care.
The study in 1991 enrolled a cross section of 1,300 American families from 10 locales across the country. The babies are followed from the age of one month through seven years.
All sorts of child-care arrangements, from formal day-care centres to stay-at-home fathers, were included in the study.
